cases.event: One spring, a long crack appeared in the fictional stone footbridge at {E}.
cases.q: What most likely caused the crack in the footbridge at {E}?
restate: A crack appeared in the footbridge at {E}, and the question asks why.
Something caused the stone footbridge at {E} to crack one spring.
cases.answer: Soil washing out from under one abutment most likely caused the crack at {E}, because the arch lost the firm support it needs at that end.
cases.sum: the evidence points to the washed-out soil under the abutment as the cause of the crack.
cases.myth: The footbridge at {E} cracked because its stones grew tired of carrying people.
cases.mythClause: the crack appeared only on days when trucks crossed
cases.cause: the washed-out soil under the abutment
cases.altText: Some residents suggested that heavy trucks had been crossing the footbridge at {E}.
cases.patternQ: What pattern connects the support under the abutment and the crack at {E}?
cases.patternA: The crack appeared after soil washed out from under the abutment and stopped growing once the support was rebuilt, so the crack followed the support.
cases.patternSum: the crack appeared when the soil washed out and stopped growing once the support was rebuilt.

obs.text: Engineers found a hollow space where soil had washed out from under the west abutment.
exps: an abutment with nothing firm beneath it cannot push back against the arch, so the stones shift and crack
this shows how the bridge lost its support, since the soil under one end was gone

obs.text: After workers packed new soil and stone under the abutment, the crack stopped growing within {n1} weeks.

fixing the support fixed the problem, so the two are linked
once the cause was repaired, the effect stopped
